chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn that some of our companions wrote to Abu al-Hasan al-Madi (peace be upon him) asking him about prayer on glass.

He said: When my letter reached him, I pondered and said to myself, 'It is something that the earth produces, so I do not need to ask him about it.' He said: He wrote to me, 'Do not pray on glass, even if your soul tells you that it is from what the earth produces. However, it is from salt and sand, and they are metamorphosed.'

key_terms.الْمَاضِي: The previous one (referring to an Imam)
key_terms.مَمْسُوخَانِ: Metamorphosed (having undergone a change in form/nature)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to perform prayer on glass according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Hadi (AS) addresses a specific legal query about praying on glass, clarifying that despite its earthly appearance, its composition of salt and sand renders it 'metamorphosed' (masukh) and thus distinct from the pure earth required for sajdah. This ruling highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the physical purity and origin of the prostration surface, distinguishing between natural earth and processed materials. The Imam’s reasoning underscores the principle that suitability for worship depends on the substance's essential nature rather than its superficial resemblance to earth.

en.sarwar: 14. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn who has said the following: “Certain ones of our people wrote to abu al-Hassan, the previous one, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, asking about Salah (prayer) on glass.

He has said that when my letter finished I thought and said to myself that it is something that grows from earth, so I do not need to write and ask him (the Imam). He (the Imam) wrote to me, ‘You must not perform Salah (prayer) on glass even though your soul has spoken to you that it is of what earth grows. However, it is from salt and sand and they both are metamorphosed.’”
